rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 1 of 3, on two ropes, down the south face to the Pernod-Chablis notch. A single 70 m just barely works; a single 60 m leaves you several metres short.
rappel_detail.anchor: two-piton station equalized with cord (or a slung horn)
hazards: Rope-eating cracks sit a few feet below the slung-horn station: build that anchor as high as practical so the rope does not jam on the pull.
rappel_detail.station: The summit area. The short aid block just below the top has one newer bolt and one old quarter-inch bolt with an aging hanger; do not trust the old bolt alone.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 2 of 3, double-rope, down Chablis’s East Face line.
rappel_detail.anchor: anchor at the top of the Chablis East Face rappel line
rappel_detail.station: From the notch, a short 4th-class scramble regains the East Face rappel line on Chablis.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 3 of 3, double-rope, to the base.
rappel_detail.anchor: next station on the Chablis East Face line
rappel_detail.station: The next station down the Chablis line.

wa_south_face_2.rappels: 3 double-rope rappels (two 60 m ropes): one down Pernod’s south face to the Pernod-Chablis notch, then two down the Chablis East Face line to the base
wa_south_face_2.descent_text: This is not a walk-off — the way down is by rappel. From the summit area, one commonly used anchor is a two-piton station equalized with cord; the short aid block just below the top is protected by a mix of one newer bolt and one old quarter-inch bolt with an aging hanger — treat the old bolt with real suspicion. Rappel the south face to the Pernod-Chablis notch on two ropes (60m ropes recommended; a single 70m can just barely work, but a 60m single can leave you several meters short of the notch). Watch for rope-eating cracks a few feet below a slung-horn rap station — build that anchor as high as practical so the rope doesn't jam on the pull. From the notch, a short 4th-class scramble regains the East Face rappel line on Chablis, and two double-rope rappels down that line reach the base, rather than re-climbing back over to Burgundy Col. If you're descending independently instead of via Chablis, reverse the traverse below Chianti back to Burgundy Col and follow the climbers' path down the scree gullies to the bench camp and boot path to the highway.

ab_professor_falls_area_the_professor_fa.rappels: Bolted rappel stations on each tier; one 60 m or 70 m rope is enough, though two ropes make it easier.

az_abracadaver.rappels: Rappel the line of ascent with two ropes.
az_abracadaver.descent_text: Rappel the route itself using two ropes.

wa_sahale_mountain_r1.rappels: One short rappel (~30m, single rope) off tat/sling anchors on the summit block down to the col; some parties instead continue south to the Sahale Glacier via a longer second rappel (two 30m ropes or a 60m doubled).
wa_sahale_mountain_r1.descent_text: Most parties reverse the col traverse and Quien Sabe Glacier back down to Boston Basin camp, staying roped through the crevassed midsection and re-negotiating the two snow-bridge crossings near 8,100 ft and 7,600 ft. Coming off the true summit block itself typically involves one short rappel rather than a downclimb - commonly to the southeast/south off the summit block on tat/slings at a natural anchor, dropping onto easier class 3 terrain; a single 30m rope is generally sufficient for this short rappel, though confident parties without rope sometimes downclimb the class 3-4 moves in reverse instead. Some parties skip reversing the technical col/glacier terrain and instead continue down the south side into the Sahale Glacier basin (as on the standard Sahale Arm route), which involves a second, longer rappel - two 30m ropes, or a single 60m rope doubled, off tat anchors on the south face - down to a ledge, followed by a short 3rd-class downscramble to the Sahale Glacier, then a hike out via the Sahale Arm/Cascade Pass Trail. Either way, expect real crevasse hazard on the glacier descent that increases through the season, plus loose, chossy rock on the south-side downscramble option.

wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.rappels: ~5 rappels with a single 60 m rope (about 3 with two ropes), reversing the route down the ridge and couloir to the Quien Sabe Glacier
wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.rappel_count_note: This count covers the couloir as well as the ridge above the notch. A published route description gives about five rappels, descending by rappelling and downclimbing the route. A two-rope party logged three — 20 m into the gully, 10 m to the belay anchor, then a final 30 m rappel to the Quien Sabe Glacier, using both ropes for the last. Anchors along this line are documented as blocky and inconsistent — inspect before trusting.
wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ridge: downclimb the upper class 4 crest a short distance (commonly cited as roughly 20 ft) to a chockstone/horn or fixed tat-and-ring station near the top of the gully, then rappel and downclimb the rest of the way back to the glacier along essentially the same line you climbed. Trip reports converge on roughly 4–5 rappels total to get from the ridge back down through the gully to the Quien Sabe Glacier — a short rappel or two off the upper ridge to regain the notch/gully, followed by two or three longer rappels down the couloir itself (some parties do the gully in two long raps of ~30 m each using two ropes tied together or doubled, others break it into shorter 15–20 m pitches on natural anchors). A single 60 m rope is generally enough for any individual station, and doubling/joining two ropes lets you skip stations in the gully if you're moving as a pair. Anchors are a mix of fixed tat-and-ring stations left by prior parties, slung chockstones and horns, and at least one station reported built from a couple of old pitons — quality is inconsistent and should not be trusted blindly. This matters here specifically: a well-documented 2005 accident on this exact descent involved a single-point natural anchor (one cordelette/webbing around a loose block, no backup) that failed under a multi-person rappel and resulted in three fatalities. Back up marginal anchors, rappel one at a time where anchors are questionable, and expect loose/blocky rock and, in shoulder season, wet rope and snow/ice in the gully. Once back on the Quien Sabe Glacier, downclimb/walk the snowfields back to camp, reversing the approach.
